text:
“Let me punish myself. I too am guilty. Do you want me to withdraw to La Trappe? The austerity of that life may appease your God...
Ah, heavens! If only I could take Stanislas’s illness upon myself...

“Ah! You do love him,” said Madame de Rênal, rising and throwing herself into his arms.

At that very moment, she pushed him away in horror.

“I believe you! I believe you!” she continued, after sinking to her knees again; “oh, my only friend! Oh, why are you not Stanislas’s father? Then it would not be a horrible sin to love you more than your son.

“Will you allow me to stay, and from now on to love you only as a brother? It is the only reasonable atonement; it may appease the wrath of the Most High.”

“And I,” she cried, rising and taking Julien’s head between her two hands, and holding it before her eyes at arm’s length, “shall I love you as a brother? Is it within my power to love you as a brother?”

Julien dissolved into tears.

“I shall obey you,” he said, falling at her feet, “I shall obey you whatever you command me; that is all that remains for me to do. My mind has been struck blind; I can see no course to take. If I leave you, you tell your husband everything, you ruin yourself and him along with you. After this ridicule, he will never be appointed a deputy. If I stay, you believe me to be the cause of your son’s death, and you die of grief. Do you want to try the effect of my departure? If you wish, I shall go and punish myself for our transgression by leaving you for a week. I shall spend it in whatever retreat you choose. At the abbey of Bray-le-Haut, for example: but swear to me that during my absence you will confess nothing to your husband. Bear in mind that I shall no longer be able to return if you speak.”

She promised; he left, but was called back after two days.

“It is impossible for me to keep my oath without you. I shall speak to my husband unless you are constantly here to command me with your eyes to remain silent. Every hour of this abominable life seems to me to last a whole day.”

At last heaven took pity on this unhappy mother. Little by little, Stanislas was no longer in danger. But the ice had been broken; her reason had become aware of the full extent of her sin: she could no longer regain her equilibrium. Remorse remained, and it was what it had to be in so sincere a heart. Her life was heaven and hell: hell when she did not see Julien, heaven when she was at his feet.

“I no longer harbor any illusions,” she would tell him, even at moments when she dared surrender herself to all her love; “I am damned, irresistibly damned. You are young; you yielded to my enticements; heaven may forgive you, but I am damned. I know it by a sure sign. I am afraid: who would not be afraid at the sight of hell? But deep down, I do not repent at all. I would commit my transgression again if it were there to be committed. If only heaven does not punish me in this world, and through my children, I shall have more than I deserve. But you, at least, my Julien,” she would cry at other moments, “are you happy? Do you find that I love you enough?”

Julien’s mistrust and wounded pride, which above all needed a love that made sacrifices, could not hold out before the sight of so great, so unquestionable a sacrifice, made at every instant. He adored Madame de Rênal. She may be noble, and I the son of a workman, but she loves me... With her, I am not a valet charged with performing the duties of a lover. Once this fear had been dispelled, Julien fell into all the follies of love, into its deadly uncertainties.

“At least,” she would cry when she saw his doubts about her love, “let me make you truly happy during the few days we have to spend together! Let us hurry; tomorrow, perhaps, I shall no longer be yours. If heaven strikes me through my children, it will be in vain that I try to live only to love you, not to see that it is my crime that is killing them. I shall not be able to survive that blow. Even if I wished to, I could not; I would go mad.

“Ah! If only I could take your sin upon myself, as you so generously offered to take Stanislas’s raging fever upon yourself!”

This great moral crisis changed the nature of the feeling that united Julien with his mistress. His love was no longer merely admiration for her beauty, the pride of possessing her.

Their happiness was henceforth of a far higher nature; the flame that consumed them became more intense. They had transports filled with madness. Their happiness would have appeared greater in the eyes of the world. But they never again found the delightful serenity, the cloudless felicity, the easy happiness of the first stages of their love, when Madame de Rênal’s only fear was that Julien did not love her enough. Their happiness sometimes bore the countenance of crime.

At the happiest and apparently calmest moments:

“Ah! Great God! I see hell,” Madame de Rênal would suddenly cry, gripping Julien’s hand with a convulsive movement. “What horrible torments! I have well deserved them.”

She would clasp him tightly, clinging to him like ivy to a wall.

Julien tried in vain to calm that agitated soul. She would take his hand and cover it with kisses. Then, falling back into a dark reverie:

“Hell,” she would say, “hell would be a mercy to me; I would still have a few days on earth to spend with him, but hell in this world itself, the death of my children... And yet, at that price, perhaps my crime would be forgiven... Ah! Great God! Do not grant me mercy at that price. These poor children have not offended You; I, I have. I alone am guilty! I love a man who is not my husband.”

Julien would then see Madame de Rênal reach moments of apparent calm. She tried to master herself; she did not want to poison the life of the one she loved.

Amid these alternations of love, remorse, and pleasure, the days passed for them with the speed of lightning. Julien lost the habit of thinking.

Mademoiselle Élisa went to attend to a minor lawsuit she had in Verrières. She found Monsieur Valenod deeply incensed against Julien. She hated the tutor and often spoke to him about Julien.
